Appendix A Theoretical Analysis

This appendix formalizes a mechanism behind Cognitive Pairwise Training (CPT). The analysis links four ideas: pairwise trace comparison can shape a reusable reliability boundary; this boundary can transfer from externally judged traces to the model’s own generations; trace-level reliability can translate into query-level abstention; and subsequent RL need not erase the boundary when policy drift is controlled. We state the results as propositions because each step depends on explicit structural assumptions, and we keep those assumptions visible throughout the argument.

A.1 Setup and Notation

Definition 1 (Problem, trace, and latent reliability class).

Let x∼𝒳x\sim\mathcal{X} be a problem instance, let a∗a^{\ast} be its reference answer available to the data constructor or teacher judge, and let τ∈𝒯\tau\in\mathcal{T} denote a reasoning trace. We write

Y⋆​(x,a∗,τ)∈{+,−}Y^{\star}(x,a^{\ast},\tau)\in\{+,-\}

for the oracle/teacher-side latent reliability class, where ++ means the trace is acceptable and −- means it is unacceptable. This binary class is a modeling abstraction that compresses the teacher judge’s four evaluation dimensions (correctness, logical soundness, clarity, and efficiency) into a single acceptability variable relevant to abstention. Importantly, a∗a^{\ast} is used to define supervision and evaluation labels; it is not an input to the model-side internal monitor at inference time. When no confusion arises, we write YY for Y⋆Y^{\star}.

Definition 2 (Four-way pairwise label space).

CPT trains on inputs

u=(x,a∗,τA,τB)u=(x,a^{\ast},\tau^{A},\tau^{B})

and outputs one of four labels

𝒴={A≻B,B≻A,eq​-​good,eq​-​bad}.\mathcal{Y}=\{A\succ B,\;B\succ A,\;\mathrm{eq\text{-}good},\;\mathrm{eq\text{-}bad}\}.

This matches the actual annotation protocol in the method section: the teacher judge compares two traces and may output a strict preference, or declare that both traces are similarly good or similarly bad.

Definition 3 (Representation and trace-level discriminator).

Let

𝐳=ϕθ​(x,τ)∈𝒵\mathbf{z}=\phi_{\theta}(x,\tau)\in\mathcal{Z}

be the model-accessible hidden representation of a single trace. We endow 𝒵\mathcal{Z} with a norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| (typically 𝒵=ℝd\mathcal{Z}=\mathbb{R}^{d} with dd the backbone hidden size and ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| the Euclidean norm). A trace-level discriminator is a measurable function

dϕ:𝒵→ℝ,d_{\phi}:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R},

where 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is the representation space. With an acceptance threshold t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, dϕd_{\phi} induces the binary monitor

h(𝐳)=𝟏[dϕ(𝐳)≥t],h(\mathbf{z})=\mathbf{1}[d_{\phi}(\mathbf{z})\geq t],

where h⁡(𝐳)=1h(\mathbf{z})=1 means “accept / sufficiently reliable” and h⁡(𝐳)=0h(\mathbf{z})=0 means “reject / unreliable.”

Remark (Externalized supervision and internalized monitoring).

The reference answer a∗a^{\ast} belongs to the externalized teacher/evaluation channel: it helps construct Y⋆Y^{\star} and the pairwise labels. The monitor analyzed below is internal to the policy because it depends only on ϕθ​(x,τ)\phi_{\theta}(x,\tau) at inference time. The analysis therefore treats CPT as an internalization process: supervision is built with teacher-side information, while the resulting reliability boundary is expressed in model-accessible representations.

Remark (Analytical role of dϕd_{\phi}).

The score dϕd_{\phi} is an analytical latent score over model-accessible trace representations. It represents the quality-sensitive direction that CPT can shape through comparison training, whether or not it is implemented as a separate architectural head.

A.2 Why Pairwise Comparison May Help

Remark (Pairwise supervision reduces the burden of absolute calibration).

CPT supervises comparative judgment rather than direct pointwise scoring. This can be easier for two reasons. First, the model need not calibrate a global absolute quality scale over all traces; it only needs to decide which of two traces is more reliable, or whether both are similarly good or bad. Second, presenting two candidate traces side by side makes discriminative features—such as algebraic consistency, unsupported transitions, or circular reasoning—more salient than in isolated pointwise evaluation. Pairwise supervision therefore provides a natural route for learning trace-quality discrimination.

A.3 Proposition 1: A Shared Discriminant View of the Four-Way CPT Task

The first question is how the actual four-label CPT task can be connected to a reusable trace-level monitor without rewriting the method into a pure reward-model story.

Assumption 1 (Shared discriminant model for four-way judgments).

There exist a model-side trace-level discriminator dϕ:𝒵→ℝd_{\phi}:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}, a threshold t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, and a margin γ≥0\gamma\geq 0 such that pairwise labels on external traces are generated by the following rule: Let dA≜dϕ​(𝐳A)d_{A}\triangleq d_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}^{A}) and dB≜dϕ​(𝐳B)d_{B}\triangleq d_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}^{B}), where 𝐳A=ϕθ​(x,τA)\mathbf{z}^{A}=\phi_{\theta}(x,\tau^{A}) and 𝐳B=ϕθ​(x,τB)\mathbf{z}^{B}=\phi_{\theta}(x,\tau^{B}). The teacher may use a∗a^{\ast} to define the label, but the score being internalized is evaluated on the model-accessible trace representation. The pair label is generated by

gϕ​(x,a∗,τA,τB)=A≻B\displaystyle g_{\phi}(x,a^{\ast},\tau^{A},\tau^{B})=A\succ B ⇔dA≥dB+γ,\displaystyle\iff d_{A}\geq d_{B}+\gamma,
gϕ​(x,a∗,τA,τB)=B≻A\displaystyle g_{\phi}(x,a^{\ast},\tau^{A},\tau^{B})=B\succ A ⇔dB≥dA+γ,\displaystyle\iff d_{B}\geq d_{A}+\gamma,
gϕ​(x,a∗,τA,τB)=eq​-​good\displaystyle g_{\phi}(x,a^{\ast},\tau^{A},\tau^{B})=\mathrm{eq\text{-}good} ⇔|dA−dB|<γ​ and ​min⁡(dA,dB)≥t,\displaystyle\iff|d_{A}-d_{B}|<\gamma\text{ and }\min(d_{A},d_{B})\geq t,
gϕ​(x,a∗,τA,τB)=eq​-​bad\displaystyle g_{\phi}(x,a^{\ast},\tau^{A},\tau^{B})=\mathrm{eq\text{-}bad} ⇔|dA−dB|<γ​ and ​max⁡(dA,dB)<t.\displaystyle\iff|d_{A}-d_{B}|<\gamma\text{ and }\max(d_{A},d_{B})<t.

The assumption captures the case in which four-way comparisons are organized by a shared trace-level discriminant. In that case, the comparison task and a single-trace reliability monitor are formally compatible.

Proposition 1 (Pairwise supervision is compatible with a reusable reliability boundary).

Under Assumption 1, the same function h(𝐳)=𝟏[dϕ(𝐳)≥t]h(\mathbf{z})=\mathbf{1}[d_{\phi}(\mathbf{z})\geq t] simultaneously supports the following conclusions on external traces:

  1. 1.

    If the pair label is eq​-​good\mathrm{eq\text{-}good}, then both traces are accepted: h⁡(𝐳A)=h⁡(𝐳B)=1h(\mathbf{z}^{A})=h(\mathbf{z}^{B})=1.

  2. 2.

    If the pair label is eq​-​bad\mathrm{eq\text{-}bad}, then both traces are rejected: h⁡(𝐳A)=h⁡(𝐳B)=0h(\mathbf{z}^{A})=h(\mathbf{z}^{B})=0.

  3. 3.

    If a strict-preference pair crosses the acceptance boundary, i.e., one trace satisfies dϕ​(𝐳)≥td_{\phi}(\mathbf{z})\geq t and the other satisfies dϕ​(𝐳)<td_{\phi}(\mathbf{z})<t, then the preferred trace is accepted and the dispreferred trace is rejected.

In particular, the four-way CPT task can be viewed as training signals that constrain a shared trace-level reliability boundary, rather than requiring pairwise supervision to be reduced to an explicit pointwise reward-model objective.

Proof.

Items (1) and (2) follow directly from the definitions of eq​-​good\mathrm{eq\text{-}good} and eq​-​bad\mathrm{eq\text{-}bad} in Assumption 1. For item (3), suppose without loss of generality that gϕg_{\phi} outputs A≻BA\succ B and that the pair crosses the threshold, so dϕ​(𝐳A)≥t>dϕ​(𝐳B)d_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}^{A})\geq t>d_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}^{B}). Then by definition h⁡(𝐳A)=1h(\mathbf{z}^{A})=1 and h⁡(𝐳B)=0h(\mathbf{z}^{B})=0. The case B≻AB\succ A is symmetric. Therefore the same threshold rule hh is consistent with equal-good, equal-bad, and cross-threshold strict-preference supervision. ∎

Discussion.

Proposition 1 isolates the part of pairwise supervision that is most relevant to metacognition: comparison labels can shape a reusable quality-sensitive boundary in representation space. The margin γ\gamma in Assumption 1 is important for the next step. When two traces have similar scores, the eq-good/eq-bad labels tie their shared quality to the threshold tt; when scores differ by at least γ\gamma, strict preferences provide directional separation. Together, these signals encourage a boundary with non-trivial score margin around reliable and unreliable traces.

A.4 Proposition 2: External-to-Internal Transfer via Boundary Stability

Once a trace-level monitor is shaped on externally judged traces, the key question is why the same boundary should remain useful on the model’s own generations. The answer comes from three structural premises: self-generated traces stay locally coupled to external traces within the same reliability class, the score varies smoothly in representation space, and little external mass lies near the decision boundary. These premises yield a classifier-level transfer bound for the same monitor.

A.4.1 Structural assumptions

Assumption 2 (Local perturbation and boundary regularity).

To explain why external discrimination remains valid internally, we assume that self-generated traces act as local perturbations of external traces within the same quality class, and that the learned boundary is stable. Formally, for the norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| on 𝒵\mathcal{Z}:

  1. 1.

    Within-class local coupling. For each class c∈{+,−}c\in\{+,-\}, let Zcext∼PcextZ^{\mathrm{ext}}_{c}\sim P^{\mathrm{ext}}_{c} and Zcself∼PcselfZ^{\mathrm{self}}_{c}\sim P^{\mathrm{self}}_{c} denote the representation distributions of external and self-generated traces conditioned on Y=cY=c. There exists a coupling πc\pi_{c} of (Zcext,Zcself)(Z^{\mathrm{ext}}_{c},Z^{\mathrm{self}}_{c}) and parameters ρc≥0\rho_{c}\geq 0, δc∈[0,1]\delta_{c}\in[0,1] such that

    ℙπc[∥Zcself−Zcext∥>ρc]≤δc.\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{c}}\!\left[\,\|Z^{\mathrm{self}}_{c}-Z^{\mathrm{ext}}_{c}\|>\rho_{c}\,\right]\leq\delta_{c}.

    Intuitively, conditioned on the same latent reliability class, a self-generated trace is represented as a local deformation of some external trace, rather than as a sample from an unrelated region of representation space. This premise matches the main Qwen pipeline: the comparison traces are rolled out from Qwen3-4B/8B/14B models, the downstream policies are Qwen3 models at the same or nearby scales, and the SFT warm-start traces are generated by a Qwen3 teacher. These design choices make the CPT-trained policy’s own rollouts natural variations of the externally judged trace family.

  2. 2.

    Lipschitz regularity of the score. There exists L>0L>0 such that the scalar score dϕd_{\phi} is LL-Lipschitz:

    |dϕ​(𝐳)−dϕ​(𝐳′)|≤L​‖𝐳−𝐳′‖∀𝐳,𝐳′∈𝒵.|d_{\phi}(\mathbf{z})-d_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}^{\prime})|\leq L\,\|\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{z}^{\prime}\|\qquad\forall\,\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Z}.
  3. 3.

    Boundary-mass function. For each class c∈{+,−}c\in\{+,-\} and radius r≥0r\geq 0, define the class-conditional boundary-mass function

    μc(r)≜ℙZ∼Pcext[|dϕ(Z)−t|≤r].\mu_{c}(r)\triangleq\mathbb{P}_{Z\sim P^{\mathrm{ext}}_{c}}\!\bigl[\,|d_{\phi}(Z)-t|\leq r\,\bigr].

    This quantity measures how much class-cc external mass lies within an rr-neighborhood of the decision boundary. A small μc​(r)\mu_{c}(r) says that most class-cc points enjoy a non-trivial score margin from the threshold.

Remark (Interpretation of the structural premises).

The three premises separate different parts of the mechanism.

  • •

    Item (1) is local and class-conditional: it controls how far a typical self-generated representation moves from a same-class external representation in norm.

  • •

    Item (2) is a regularity property of the score: if representations move only locally, the scalar score cannot jump arbitrarily.

  • •

    Item (3) links back to the margin γ\gamma in Assumption 1: pairwise labels encourage reliable and unreliable traces to lie away from the threshold, so the external mass in a narrow boundary band is small.

Together, local coupling, score regularity, and low boundary mass imply that the monitor’s decision changes only on a controlled set of examples.

Definition 4 ((α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-discrimination).

For a fixed threshold rule h(𝐳)=𝟏[dϕ(𝐳)≥t]h(\mathbf{z})=\mathbf{1}[d_{\phi}(\mathbf{z})\geq t], define the miss rate

α=ℙ[h(𝐳)=0∣Y=+]\alpha=\mathbb{P}[h(\mathbf{z})=0\mid Y=+]

and the false-acceptance rate

β=ℙ[h(𝐳)=1∣Y=−].\beta=\mathbb{P}[h(\mathbf{z})=1\mid Y=-].

We write (αext,βext)(\alpha_{\mathrm{ext}},\beta_{\mathrm{ext}}) for the error rates evaluated on external traces, and (αself,βself)(\alpha_{\mathrm{self}},\beta_{\mathrm{self}}) for those on self-generated traces, both using the same threshold tt.

A.4.2 Main transfer statement

Proposition 2 (Boundary stability under local source shift).

Suppose the external trace-level monitor hh achieves (αext,βext)(\alpha_{\mathrm{ext}},\beta_{\mathrm{ext}})-discrimination on external traces. Under Assumption 2, the same monitor on self-generated traces satisfies

αself\displaystyle\alpha_{\mathrm{self}} ≤αext+δ++μ+​(L​ρ+),\displaystyle\leq\alpha_{\mathrm{ext}}+\delta_{+}+\mu_{+}(L\rho_{+}),
βself\displaystyle\beta_{\mathrm{self}} ≤βext+δ−+μ−​(L​ρ−).\displaystyle\leq\beta_{\mathrm{ext}}+\delta_{-}+\mu_{-}(L\rho_{-}).

Consequently,

αself+βself≤αext+βext+δ++δ−+μ+​(L​ρ+)+μ−​(L​ρ−).\alpha_{\mathrm{self}}+\beta_{\mathrm{self}}\;\leq\;\alpha_{\mathrm{ext}}+\beta_{\mathrm{ext}}+\delta_{+}+\delta_{-}+\mu_{+}(L\rho_{+})+\mu_{-}(L\rho_{-}).
Proof.

We prove the α\alpha bound; the β\beta bound is symmetric.

Fix the class c=+c=+ and let π+\pi_{+} be the coupling from Assumption 2.1. Define the events on the coupled pair (Z+ext,Z+self)(Z^{\mathrm{ext}}_{+},Z^{\mathrm{self}}_{+}):

Eclose≜{∥Z+self−Z+ext∥≤ρ+},Emargin≜{|dϕ(Z+ext)−t|>Lρ+}.E_{\mathrm{close}}\triangleq\bigl\{\|Z^{\mathrm{self}}_{+}-Z^{\mathrm{ext}}_{+}\|\leq\rho_{+}\bigr\},\qquad E_{\mathrm{margin}}\triangleq\bigl\{|d_{\phi}(Z^{\mathrm{ext}}_{+})-t|>L\rho_{+}\bigr\}.

Step 1 (on Eclose∩EmarginE_{\mathrm{close}}\cap E_{\mathrm{margin}} the monitor cannot disagree). On EcloseE_{\mathrm{close}}, Assumption 2.2 yields

|dϕ​(Z+self)−dϕ​(Z+ext)|≤L​‖Z+self−Z+ext‖≤L​ρ+.|d_{\phi}(Z^{\mathrm{self}}_{+})-d_{\phi}(Z^{\mathrm{ext}}_{+})|\leq L\,\|Z^{\mathrm{self}}_{+}-Z^{\mathrm{ext}}_{+}\|\leq L\rho_{+}.

On EmarginE_{\mathrm{margin}} the external score is at distance strictly greater than L​ρ+L\rho_{+} from the threshold tt. Combining the two, the self-generated score lies on the same side of tt as the external score, which is exactly h⁡(Z+self)=h⁡(Z+ext)h(Z^{\mathrm{self}}_{+})=h(Z^{\mathrm{ext}}_{+}).

Step 2 (decompose the α\alpha gap through the coupling). By the definition of α\alpha and the coupling π+\pi_{+}, we express both error rates as expectations over the same coupling:

αext=𝔼π+[𝟏{h(Z+ext)=0}],αself=𝔼π+[𝟏{h(Z+self)=0}].\alpha_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{+}}\!\bigl[\mathbf{1}\{h(Z^{\mathrm{ext}}_{+})=0\}\bigr],\qquad\alpha_{\mathrm{self}}=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{+}}\!\bigl[\mathbf{1}\{h(Z^{\mathrm{self}}_{+})=0\}\bigr].

Define the disagreement event Edis={h(Z+self)≠h(Z+ext)}E_{\mathrm{dis}}=\{h(Z^{\mathrm{self}}_{+})\neq h(Z^{\mathrm{ext}}_{+})\}. Since {h(Z+self)=0}⊆{h(Z+ext)=0}∪Edis\{h(Z^{\mathrm{self}}_{+})=0\}\subseteq\{h(Z^{\mathrm{ext}}_{+})=0\}\cup E_{\mathrm{dis}}, taking probabilities under π+\pi_{+} gives

αself≤ℙπ+[h(Z+ext)=0]+ℙπ+[Edis]=αext+ℙπ+[Edis].\alpha_{\mathrm{self}}\;\leq\;\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{+}}[h(Z^{\mathrm{ext}}_{+})=0]\;+\;\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{+}}[E_{\mathrm{dis}}]\;=\;\alpha_{\mathrm{ext}}+\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{+}}[E_{\mathrm{dis}}].

Step 3 (bound the disagreement probability). By Step 1, a disagreement can occur only if Eclose∩EmarginE_{\mathrm{close}}\cap E_{\mathrm{margin}} fails. A union bound gives

ℙπ+​[Edis]≤ℙπ+​[Eclosec]+ℙπ+​[Emarginc]≤δ++μ+​(L​ρ+),\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{+}}[E_{\mathrm{dis}}]\;\leq\;\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{+}}[E_{\mathrm{close}}^{c}]\;+\;\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{+}}[E_{\mathrm{margin}}^{c}]\;\leq\;\delta_{+}\;+\;\mu_{+}(L\rho_{+}),

where the first term uses Assumption 2.1 and the second term uses Assumption 2.3 together with the fact that the marginal of π+\pi_{+} on Z+extZ^{\mathrm{ext}}_{+} is P+extP^{\mathrm{ext}}_{+}, so

ℙπ+[Emarginc]=ℙP+ext[|dϕ(Z)−t|≤Lρ+]=μ+(Lρ+).\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{+}}[E_{\mathrm{margin}}^{c}]=\mathbb{P}_{P^{\mathrm{ext}}_{+}}\!\bigl[|d_{\phi}(Z)-t|\leq L\rho_{+}\bigr]=\mu_{+}(L\rho_{+}).

Combining Steps 2–3 proves αself≤αext+δ++μ+​(L​ρ+)\alpha_{\mathrm{self}}\leq\alpha_{\mathrm{ext}}+\delta_{+}+\mu_{+}(L\rho_{+}). The argument for β\beta is identical with class −- in place of ++. ∎

Discussion.

Proposition 2 identifies the geometric mechanism behind external-to-internal transfer. Within each reliability class, self-generated traces stay near externally judged traces; the score changes smoothly under local representation perturbations; and CPT encourages a margin around the reliability threshold. The resulting bound has two interpretable error terms: coupling failure (δ±\delta_{\pm}), when a self-generated trace leaves the local neighborhood of its class, and boundary ambiguity (μ±​(L​ρ±)\mu_{\pm}(L\rho_{\pm})), when the corresponding external representation already lies near the decision threshold.

A.4.3 A 1-D score-marginal corollary and a clean special case

Proposition 2 also admits a one-dimensional formulation in terms of the scalar discriminator marginal. Let μcext\mu^{\mathrm{ext}}_{c} and μcself\mu^{\mathrm{self}}_{c} denote the pushforward distributions of dϕ​(𝐳)d_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}) on ℝ\mathbb{R} under PcextP^{\mathrm{ext}}_{c} and PcselfP^{\mathrm{self}}_{c} respectively.

Corollary 1 (Score-marginal form).

Under Assumption 2, the one-dimensional score marginals satisfy

|μcself({d<t})−μcext({d<t})|≤δc+μc(Lρc),c∈{+,−}.\bigl|\mu^{\mathrm{self}}_{c}(\{d<t\})-\mu^{\mathrm{ext}}_{c}(\{d<t\})\bigr|\;\leq\;\delta_{c}+\mu_{c}(L\rho_{c}),\qquad c\in\{+,-\}.

Consequently, defining ηc≜δc+μc​(L​ρc)\eta_{c}\triangleq\delta_{c}+\mu_{c}(L\rho_{c}), the error-rate transfer gap is bounded by η++η−\eta_{+}+\eta_{-}.

Corollary 1 gives a one-dimensional view of the same mechanism: the monitor only uses the scalar score under class conditioning, and the external/self gap on the threshold-crossing event is bounded by ηc\eta_{c}. This form can be estimated empirically from one-dimensional score CDFs for external and self-generated traces within each class.

A second, particularly clean corollary of Proposition 2 makes the role of the margin from Proposition 1 sharper.

Corollary 2 (Uniform-margin special case).

Suppose that in addition to Assumption 2 there exist hard margins m+,m−>0m_{+},m_{-}>0 such that

μ+​(r)=0​ for all ​0≤r<m+,μ−​(r)=0​ for all ​0≤r<m−,\mu_{+}(r)=0\text{ for all }0\leq r<m_{+},\qquad\mu_{-}(r)=0\text{ for all }0\leq r<m_{-},

i.e., no external class-cc mass lies strictly within distance mcm_{c} of the threshold. If the coupling radii satisfy L​ρ+<m+L\rho_{+}<m_{+} and L​ρ−<m−L\rho_{-}<m_{-}, then

αself≤αext+δ+,βself≤βext+δ−.\alpha_{\mathrm{self}}\leq\alpha_{\mathrm{ext}}+\delta_{+},\qquad\beta_{\mathrm{self}}\leq\beta_{\mathrm{ext}}+\delta_{-}.
Proof.

Under the margin conditions, μ+​(L​ρ+)=0\mu_{+}(L\rho_{+})=0 and μ−​(L​ρ−)=0\mu_{-}(L\rho_{-})=0. The claim follows immediately from Proposition 2. ∎

Why the special case matters.

Corollary 2 makes the margin intuition explicit. When each class has a genuine score margin and the local perturbation radius is smaller than that margin, small within-class representation deformations cannot flip the monitor’s decision. Transfer then degrades only through the coupling-failure probability δc\delta_{c}, which measures how often a self-generated trace leaves the local neighborhood of its reliability class.

A.5 Proposition 3: From Trace-Level Discrimination to Query-Level Abstention

Propositions 1 and 2 operate at the trace level: they bound how well the model can classify individual reasoning traces as acceptable or unacceptable. However, the metacognitive behavior measured in our experiments is query-level abstention: given a query xx, the model either produces an answer or abstains. This subsection bridges the two levels.

Assumption 3 (Quality-driven abstention policy).

Metacognition via calibrated abstention requires the model to reject queries when its own reasoning is unreliable. We formalize this by assuming the model generates a final “abstain” response if and only if its internalized discriminator deems the generated trace τ\tau unacceptable: dϕ​(𝐳)<td_{\phi}(\mathbf{z})<t, where 𝐳=ϕθ​(x,τ)\mathbf{z}=\phi_{\theta}(x,\tau) is computed without access to a∗a^{\ast}.

For answerable queries, the generation policy yields an acceptable trace with probability γans∈(0,1]\gamma_{\mathrm{ans}}\in(0,1]. For unanswerable queries (false-premise, information-insufficient, etc.), all generated traces are intrinsically unacceptable.

This threshold rule abstracts the implicit abstention behavior that appears during autoregressive generation (e.g., producing “I don’t know” or “False premise”) into a tractable decision model. We use γans\gamma_{\mathrm{ans}} to denote the answerable-trace generation probability, distinct from the discriminator margin γ\gamma of Assumption 1.

Proposition 3 (Improved metacognition via discrimination).

Under Assumption 3, suppose CPT improves the internalized discriminator’s trace-level error rates from (αbase,βbase)(\alpha_{\mathrm{base}},\beta_{\mathrm{base}}) to (αcpt,βcpt)(\alpha_{\mathrm{cpt}},\beta_{\mathrm{cpt}}), where αcpt<αbase\alpha_{\mathrm{cpt}}<\alpha_{\mathrm{base}} and βcpt<βbase\beta_{\mathrm{cpt}}<\beta_{\mathrm{base}}. Then the query-level abstention metrics strictly improve:

Δ​Recall\displaystyle\Delta\mathrm{Recall} ≥βbase−βcpt>0,\displaystyle\geq\beta_{\mathrm{base}}-\beta_{\mathrm{cpt}}>0,
Δ​False​Abstention​Rate\displaystyle\Delta\mathrm{False\;Abstention\;Rate} ≤−γans​(αbase−αcpt)<0.\displaystyle\leq-\gamma_{\mathrm{ans}}(\alpha_{\mathrm{base}}-\alpha_{\mathrm{cpt}})<0.
Proof.

For an unanswerable query, any generated trace is unacceptable. The model correctly abstains if dϕ​(𝐳)<td_{\phi}(\mathbf{z})<t. The probability of failing to abstain (i.e., wrongly accepting the trace) is exactly the false-acceptance rate β\beta. Thus, the abstention recall is 1−β1-\beta. An improvement from βbase\beta_{\mathrm{base}} to βcpt\beta_{\mathrm{cpt}} directly yields Δ​Recall=βbase−βcpt\Delta\mathrm{Recall}=\beta_{\mathrm{base}}-\beta_{\mathrm{cpt}}.

For an answerable query, the model falsely abstains in two disjoint scenarios: (1) it generates an unacceptable trace (probability 1−γans1-\gamma_{\mathrm{ans}}) and correctly rejects it; or (2) it generates an acceptable trace (probability γans\gamma_{\mathrm{ans}}) but the discriminator falsely rejects it (probability α\alpha). The false abstention rate is (1−γans)+γans​α(1-\gamma_{\mathrm{ans}})+\gamma_{\mathrm{ans}}\alpha. Thus, the change in false abstention rate when moving from the base model to the CPT model is γans​(αcpt−αbase)\gamma_{\mathrm{ans}}(\alpha_{\mathrm{cpt}}-\alpha_{\mathrm{base}}), which is strictly negative since αcpt<αbase\alpha_{\mathrm{cpt}}<\alpha_{\mathrm{base}}. ∎

Discussion.

This proposition bridges trace-level discrimination and query-level abstention. Lower false acceptance on unreliable traces improves abstention recall on unanswerable queries, while lower miss rate on reliable traces reduces false abstention on answerable queries. In this abstraction, CPT improves abstention by strengthening the internal discrimination boundary, so the model is more likely to refuse when its reasoning trace is unreliable and more likely to answer when it has produced a reliable trace. Prompt formatting and instruction following can still modulate the observed metrics, but the direction of the trace-level effect is explicit.

A.6 Proposition 4: RL Robustness Under Trust-Region Constraints

A central empirical finding is that CPT-trained models retain abstention ability better than SFT+RL models after RL training (Figure 3). The mechanism is that RL updates may move the policy, but the learned reliability boundary remains useful when the realized movement is small. Since our GRPO-style RL uses per-step clipping, we model the update path through a trust-region condition and state the bound in terms of the realized aggregate policy drift DTD_{T}.

Assumption 4 (Trust-region constrained RL).

Let pθ0p_{\theta_{0}} be the policy after CPT + SFT. The RL stage proceeds for TT updates. We assume that the per-step marginal policy update is constrained by the trust-region clipping mechanism such that

dTV​(pθk,pθk−1)≤Δclip∀k∈{1,…,T}.d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p_{\theta_{k}},p_{\theta_{k-1}})\leq\Delta_{\mathrm{clip}}\quad\forall k\in\{1,\dots,T\}.

Define the realized aggregate drift

DT≜dTV​(pθT,pθ0).D_{T}\triangleq d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p_{\theta_{T}},p_{\theta_{0}}).

By the triangle inequality, DT≤∑k=1TdTV​(pθk,pθk−1)≤T​ΔclipD_{T}\leq\sum_{k=1}^{T}d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p_{\theta_{k}},p_{\theta_{k-1}})\leq T\Delta_{\mathrm{clip}}, but DTD_{T} can be much smaller when successive updates partially cancel or move mostly within irrelevant directions.

Assumption 5 (Minimum class priors).

We assume the probability of generating traces from either class (acceptable or unacceptable) under the initial policy pθ0p_{\theta_{0}} is bounded away from zero:

min⁡(ℙpθ0​[+],ℙpθ0​[−])≥ν>0.\min\left(\mathbb{P}_{p_{\theta_{0}}}[+],\;\mathbb{P}_{p_{\theta_{0}}}[-]\right)\geq\nu>0.

This assumption simply requires that the post-CPT model can generate both acceptable and unacceptable traces with non-negligible probability.

Proposition 4 (Bounded metacognitive degradation).

Under Assumptions 4 and 5, let (α0,β0)(\alpha_{0},\beta_{0}) be the discrimination error rates on self-generated traces after CPT, and (αT,βT)(\alpha_{T},\beta_{T}) be the rates after TT steps of RL. Let

sc≜|ℙpθT​[c]−ℙpθ0​[c]|,c∈{+,−},s_{c}\triangleq\left|\mathbb{P}_{p_{\theta_{T}}}[c]-\mathbb{P}_{p_{\theta_{0}}}[c]\right|,\qquad c\in\{+,-\},

be the class-prior drift. Assume the final class-conditional distributions are defined (for instance, DT<νD_{T}<\nu is sufficient). If the model maintains its classification threshold on the representation space, then

(αT+βT)−(α0+β0)≤2​DT+s++s−ν≤4​DTν≤4​T​Δclipν.(\alpha_{T}+\beta_{T})-(\alpha_{0}+\beta_{0})\;\leq\;\frac{2D_{T}+s_{+}+s_{-}}{\nu}\;\leq\;\frac{4D_{T}}{\nu}\;\leq\;\frac{4T\Delta_{\mathrm{clip}}}{\nu}.

In the stable-prior regime s+=s−=0s_{+}=s_{-}=0, this sharpens to

(αT+βT)−(α0+β0)≤2​DTν,(\alpha_{T}+\beta_{T})-(\alpha_{0}+\beta_{0})\;\leq\;\frac{2D_{T}}{\nu},

with the old 2​T​Δclip/ν2T\Delta_{\mathrm{clip}}/\nu expression recovered only by replacing DTD_{T} with its worst-case upper bound T​ΔclipT\Delta_{\mathrm{clip}}.

Proof.

By the event form of total variation, changes in the two error rates are bounded by class-conditional TV distances:

|αT−α0|≤dTV(pθT(𝐳∣+),pθ0(𝐳∣+)),|\alpha_{T}-\alpha_{0}|\leq d_{\mathrm{TV}}\bigl(p_{\theta_{T}}(\mathbf{z}\mid+),\;p_{\theta_{0}}(\mathbf{z}\mid+)\bigr),
|βT−β0|≤dTV(pθT(𝐳∣−),pθ0(𝐳∣−)).|\beta_{T}-\beta_{0}|\leq d_{\mathrm{TV}}\bigl(p_{\theta_{T}}(\mathbf{z}\mid-),\;p_{\theta_{0}}(\mathbf{z}\mid-)\bigr).

We next use the conditional-TV amplification bound with the class-prior correction kept explicit. Let P=pθ0P=p_{\theta_{0}}, Q=pθTQ=p_{\theta_{T}}, and fix a class cc. For any event AA in representation space,

|Q⁡(A∣c)−P⁡(A∣c)|\displaystyle|Q(A\mid c)-P(A\mid c)| =|Q⁡(A∩c)Q⁡(c)−P⁡(A∩c)P⁡(c)|\displaystyle=\left|\frac{Q(A\cap c)}{Q(c)}-\frac{P(A\cap c)}{P(c)}\right|
≤|Q⁡(A∩c)−P⁡(A∩c)|P⁡(c)+Q⁡(A∩c)​|1Q⁡(c)−1P⁡(c)|\displaystyle\leq\frac{|Q(A\cap c)-P(A\cap c)|}{P(c)}+Q(A\cap c)\left|\frac{1}{Q(c)}-\frac{1}{P(c)}\right|
≤dTV​(Q,P)P⁡(c)+|Q⁡(c)−P⁡(c)|P⁡(c).\displaystyle\leq\frac{d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Q,P)}{P(c)}+\frac{|Q(c)-P(c)|}{P(c)}.

Taking the supremum over AA and using P⁡(c)≥νP(c)\geq\nu gives

dTV​(Q⁡(𝐳∣c),P⁡(𝐳∣c))≤DT+scν.d_{\mathrm{TV}}\bigl(Q(\mathbf{z}\mid c),P(\mathbf{z}\mid c)\bigr)\leq\frac{D_{T}+s_{c}}{\nu}.

Applying this with c=+c=+ and c=−c=- yields

|αT−α0|+|βT−β0|≤2​DT+s++s−ν.|\alpha_{T}-\alpha_{0}|+|\beta_{T}-\beta_{0}|\leq\frac{2D_{T}+s_{+}+s_{-}}{\nu}.

Since (αT+βT)−(α0+β0)(\alpha_{T}+\beta_{T})-(\alpha_{0}+\beta_{0}) is bounded above by the left-hand side, the first claim follows. Finally, sc≤DTs_{c}\leq D_{T} because the class event itself is a measurable event under the same joint policy distribution, so

2​DT+s++s−ν≤4​DTν≤4​T​Δclipν.\frac{2D_{T}+s_{+}+s_{-}}{\nu}\leq\frac{4D_{T}}{\nu}\leq\frac{4T\Delta_{\mathrm{clip}}}{\nu}.

If class priors are stable, s+=s−=0s_{+}=s_{-}=0, giving the 2​DT/ν2D_{T}/\nu bound. ∎

Discussion.

Proposition 4 explains why CPT can remain stable through RL. Trust-region clipping limits each update, and the realized aggregate drift DTD_{T} measures how far the final policy actually moves from the post-CPT policy. When the initial policy generates both reliable and unreliable traces with non-negligible probability (ν>0\nu>0), small realized drift and small class-prior drift imply small class-conditional representation drift. The reliability discriminator internalized during CPT therefore remains approximately valid after RL.

Empirical plausibility.

This picture matches the RL ablation in Figure 3. In the Qwen3 series, our RL runs use about 150150 clipped updates. Under the Normal Prompt, CPT changes only mildly after RL: +0.6+0.6 F1 at 14B, −0.2-0.2 at 8B, and −0.5-0.5 at 4B. By contrast, vanilla SFT loses 1.21.2 to 2.62.6 F1 points at the same Qwen3 scales, and the 3B non-Qwen setting shows a much larger drop. These patterns are consistent with a small realized drift around the CPT-trained boundary, whereas models without CPT start from a weaker discriminator and are more easily pushed toward forced answering.

Scope of the bound.

The result should be read as a stability mechanism rather than a tight numerical predictor. Per-step clipping motivates the trust-region abstraction, while the realized drift DTD_{T} and class-prior drifts s±s_{\pm} determine the relevant post-RL change. Replacing DTD_{T} by T​ΔclipT\Delta_{\mathrm{clip}} gives a safe path-length upper envelope; the much smaller observed CPT changes indicate that the realized aggregate drift is far below this worst-case path length.

A.7 Relation to the Main Empirical Claims

Result Key assumption(s) Conclusion
Remark (§A.2) — (qualitative) Pairwise supervision reduces the burden of absolute calibration
Prop. 1 Shared discriminant model (margin γ\gamma, threshold tt) Four-way CPT labels are compatible with a reusable reliability boundary
Prop. 2 Within-class local coupling (ρ±,δ±)(\rho_{\pm},\delta_{\pm}) + LL-Lipschitz score + boundary-mass μ±\mu_{\pm} External discrimination transfers to self-monitoring with gap ≤δ++δ−+μ+​(L​ρ+)+μ−​(L​ρ−)\leq\delta_{+}+\delta_{-}+\mu_{+}(L\rho_{+})+\mu_{-}(L\rho_{-})
Cor. 2 Hard margins m±>L​ρ±m_{\pm}>L\rho_{\pm} Under a genuine margin, transfer degrades only through coupling failure δ±\delta_{\pm}
Prop. 3 Quality-driven abstention policy Lower (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) strictly improves abstention recall and reduces false abstention
Prop. 4 Realized RL drift DTD_{T} + class-prior drift s±s_{\pm} + minimum prior ν\nu Degradation ≤(2​DT+s++s−)/ν\leq(2D_{T}+s_{+}+s_{-})/\nu; worst-case ≤4​T​Δclip/ν\leq 4T\Delta_{\mathrm{clip}}/\nu

Taken together, the propositions give the following interpretation of the empirical results:

  • •

    Pairwise cognitive supervision can shape a reusable quality-sensitive boundary in representation space (Proposition 1).

  • •

    The boundary can transfer from external comparison to internal monitoring when self-generated traces stay locally coupled to externally judged traces, the score is regular, and little mass lies near the boundary (Proposition 2; Corollary 2).

  • •

    Stronger trace-level discrimination improves query-level abstention under a quality-driven abstention policy (Proposition 3).

  • •

    Subsequent RL preserves the boundary when realized policy drift and class-prior drift remain small (Proposition 4).

Thus CPT can be understood as a way to turn pairwise reasoning-quality supervision into an internal reliability boundary that remains useful for abstention and is robust to moderate post-training drift.

Appendix B Training and Data Construction Details

This section centralizes the training-side details used across the main results and ablations. All base-model runs except LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct use the same raw User:/Assistant: text format as evaluation, without using a chat template; LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct and the instruction-tuned controls keep the corresponding chat template path. SFT and GRPO are implemented on top of verl [69] 0.5.0 with project-specific support for base-model tokenization and logging. Offline DPO is implemented in-house on top of the verl FSDP SFT trainer. All experiments were completed on a 5×85\times 8 NVIDIA H20 GPU cluster (40 GPUs in total); for a 14B model under a 16-GPU allocation, the CPT stage takes approximately 17 hours, while the Math-RL stage takes approximately 50 hours.

B.1 Training Algorithms

1. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

SFT uses the verl.trainer.fsdp_sft_trainer path with FSDP, gradient checkpointing, cosine warmup scheduling and distributed checkpointing. For base checkpoints, the dataset loader extracts the raw prompt text from the stored chat-style field and tokenizes it directly, instead of applying a chat template. For LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct, we use the default settings. This keeps training prompts token-identical to the base-model evaluation and rollout prompts. The response-token negative log-likelihood is

ℒSFT​(θ)=−𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟​∑tmt​log⁡pθ​(yt∣x,y<t)∑tmt,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}\frac{\sum_{t}m_{t}\log p_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}{\sum_{t}m_{t}},

where mtm_{t} masks out prompt and padding tokens. The same SFT objective is used for Math-SFT warm start, SFT-80K, CPT, SUM-SFT, and the curated Tulu3-Mix control; these runs differ only in data and hyperparameters.

2. GRPO / MATH-RL.

The RL stage uses verl’s PPO trainer with GRPO advantages. For each prompt xx, the policy samples a group of GG responses {yi}i=1G\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G} from vLLM [39]; in the main Math-RL script G=16G=16, temperature is 0.90.9, and top-p=0.95. Rewards combine answer correctness, boxed-answer formatting, and an optional overlength penalty:

R⁡(y)=1.0⋅𝟏​[correct⁡(y)]+0.2⋅𝟏​[format⁡(y)]−0.5⋅ρlen​(y).R(y)=1.0\cdot\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{correct}(y)]+0.2\cdot\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{format}(y)]-0.5\cdot\rho_{\mathrm{len}}(y).

The length term is a DAPO-style overlong-buffer penalty:

ρlen​(y)=max⁡(0,ℓ⁡(y)−(Lmax−Lbuf)Lbuf),Lmax=12288,Lbuf=4096,\rho_{\mathrm{len}}(y)=\max\!\left(0,\frac{\ell(y)-(L_{\max}-L_{\mathrm{buf}})}{L_{\mathrm{buf}}}\right),\quad L_{\max}=12288,\;L_{\mathrm{buf}}=4096,

clipped at 11 when the response reaches the maximum generation budget. This term is used for stability rather than to encourage short answers. Directly applying RL after the warm-start SFT can enter an entropy-collapse regime. Motivated by the Just-RL [27] observation that response lengths first decrease and then increase during RL, we trace this instability to an excessive truncation rate and control it explicitly: samples that hit LmaxL_{\max} are marked as overlong, only up to 5%5\% are retained after world-size alignment, and the rest are discarded before the policy update. The soft buffer penalty and hard cap keep the effective batch from being dominated by truncated zero-reward rollouts, improving training stability and efficiency.

Correctness is checked by the same math pipeline used in evaluation: math_verify script [88] first, with GPT-4.1-mini11 1 We use OpenAI’s API model snapshot gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14; see https://platform.openai.com/docs/models/gpt-4.1-mini. semantic equivalence as fallback when enabled by the data source. The format reward is gated by a custom checker: the response must contain a valid final \boxed{} answer, keep the tail after the final box short, and avoid multi-script gibberish. To balance training stability and policy exploration, we assign this term a small weight of 0.20.2, so that it provides a lightweight parseability signal without dominating the correctness reward. Group advantages are normalized within each prompt group,

Ai=R⁡(yi)−1G​∑jR⁡(yj)stdj​(R⁡(yj))+ϵ.A_{i}=\frac{R(y_{i})-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j}R(y_{j})}{\mathrm{std}_{j}(R(y_{j}))+\epsilon}.

With token-level importance ratio ri,t=πθ​(yi,t∣x,yi,<t)/πold​(yi,t∣x,yi,<t)r_{i,t}=\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t})/\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t}), the clipped GRPO objective is

ℒGRPO(θ)=−𝔼i,t[min(ri,tAi,clip(ri,t,1−ϵℓ,1+ϵh)Ai)]+λKL𝒟KLlow​-​var(πθ∥πref),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{i,t}\!\left[\min\big(r_{i,t}A_{i},\mathrm{clip}(r_{i,t},1-\epsilon_{\ell},1+\epsilon_{h})A_{i}\big)\right]+\lambda_{\mathrm{KL}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}^{\mathrm{low\text{-}var}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}),

where ϵ=10−6\epsilon=10^{-6}, ϵℓ=0.2\epsilon_{\ell}=0.2, ϵh=0.28\epsilon_{h}=0.28, and λKL=10−3\lambda_{\mathrm{KL}}=10^{-3}. KL is optimized as an actor loss term. Entropy regularization is set to 00.

3. Offline DPO.

We implement offline DPO [61] ourselves. The trainer subclasses the verl FSDP SFT trainer and reuses its optimizer, scheduler, checkpoint manager, and logging. The only overridden components are the DPO dataset/collate path, the reference-model construction, and the training/validation steps. Each example is a triple (x,yc,yr)(x,y_{c},y_{r}) with a chosen and rejected response. The prompt is concatenated independently with each response, while the log-probability mask keeps only response tokens. A frozen reference model is loaded from the same starting checkpoint as the policy and wrapped with the same FSDP FULL_SHARD policy.

For policy log-probabilities (πc,πr)(\pi^{c},\pi^{r}) and reference log-probabilities (rc,rr)(r^{c},r^{r}) summed over response tokens, standard DPO minimizes

ℒDPO​(θ)=−𝔼​log⁡σ⁡(β⁡[(πc−πr)−(rc−rr)]),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}\log\sigma\left(\beta\left[(\pi^{c}-\pi^{r})-(r^{c}-r^{r})\right]\right),

with β=0.1\beta=0.1. The critical FSDP optimization is concatenated forward: chosen and rejected sequences are concatenated in the batch dimension and passed through each FSDP-wrapped model exactly once, then split back before the loss. This avoids the forward/backward hook-order deadlocks that arise from two separate forwards under FULL_SHARD. Reference log-probabilities are computed first under torch.no_grad(), then detached before the policy forward. Gradient accumulation is performed by per-micro-batch backward calls scaled by the number of micro-batches, followed by gradient clipping and a finite-grad-norm guard.

B.2 Training Pipelines and Datasets

All “++RL” rows use the same GRPO recipe unless explicitly stated otherwise. The data construction details are in Appendix B.4; Table 7 lists the model-level pipelines.

B.3 Training Hyperparameters

1. SFT-stage hyperparameters.

Unless noted, SFT uses two epochs, FSDP, gradient checkpointing, raw base-model prompts, and left truncation for sequence overflow. The default learning-rate rule is 3​e−53\mathrm{e}{-5} for the smallest Qwen3-4B and LLaMA-3B runs, and 1​e−51\mathrm{e}{-5} for larger models. The only SFT-stage exceptions are Qwen3-14B CPT 2×2\times (2​e−52\mathrm{e}{-5}, because the doubled corpus otherwise under-steps) and the curated Tulu3-Mix Stage-1 control (1.5​e−51.5\mathrm{e}{-5}). Table 8 gives the stage-level defaults.

2. DPO hyperparameters.

Offline DPO uses global batch 256256, max length 81928192, two epochs, learning rate 1​e−61\mathrm{e}{-6}, warmup ratio 0.10.1, β=0.1\beta=0.1, sigmoid loss, label smoothing 00, and reference_free=False.

3. GRPO hyperparameters.

Math RL uses train batch 128128, G=16G=16 rollouts per prompt, max prompt length 10241024, max response length 1228812288, temperature 0.90.9, top-p=0.95, actor FSDP2 with remove-padding and gradient checkpointing, vLLM rollout tensor parallel size 44, rollout GPU utilization 0.70.7, and max_num_batched_tokens=32768=32768. The actor uses dynamic batch sizing, token-mean loss aggregation, asymmetric PPO clipping (0.2,0.28)(0.2,0.28), KL-loss coefficient 10−310^{-3}, and entropy coefficient 00. The default RL learning rate is 1​e−61\mathrm{e}{-6} across final runs. Overlong responses are penalized in the last 40964096 tokens with maximum penalty 0.50.5 and can be dropped, while keeping at most 5%5\% overlong samples for stability. For every RL run, we select the checkpoint with the best validation math accuracy, where validation is the union of the seven math evaluation sets and uses one rollout per problem.

B.4 Training Data Construction

This section documents how the training data used in the paper is constructed. We first describe the three seed problem pools that serve as the backbone for the downstream datasets (§B.4.1), and then specify how each SFT or DPO corpus is assembled: Math-SFT (§B.4.2), SFT-80K (§B.4.3), the CPT data-scaling variants 0.5×\times/2×\times (§B.4.5), the SUM-SFT abstention baseline (§B.4.6), and the DPO preference pools (§B.4.7). We close with the two RL training sets: Abstention-RL 5K (§B.4.8) and Math-RL (§B.4.9). The main CPT corpus is summarized in §3.1, with reproduction details provided below. To keep the section non-redundant we centralize two recurring conventions:

  • •

    Difficulty stratification. Every problem is binned into four buckets (easy / medium / hard / very_hard) by the pass rate of Qwen3-4B-Base under 2020 probing rollouts, with thresholds >0.8>\!0.8 / [0.5,0.8][0.5,0.8] / [0.2,0.5)[0.2,0.5) / <0.2<\!0.2.

  • •

    Teacher sampling temperatures. Unless explicitly noted otherwise, all teacher-model generation in this paper follows two fixed presets: single-shot T=0.3T{=}0.3 (one rollout per item; used whenever we want a single high-quality answer trace, e.g. SFT path generation, SUM CoT generation) and multi-shot T=0.7T{=}0.7 (many rollouts per item; used whenever we want a diverse pool, e.g. the 1212-rollout expansion pool, the K=8K{=}8 self-consistency teacher-judge, or multi-rollout pair construction). top-p=0.95p{=}0.95, top-k=20k{=}20, max_tokens=8,192=8{,}192 throughout. The teacher policy is Qwen3-235B-Instruct-2507 [60] unless stated otherwise. Verification of generated answers uses the two-stage pipeline documented in §B.4.4: math_verify first, with GPT-4.1-mini as a semantic-equivalence fallback.

B.4.1 Three Seed Problem Pools

All downstream training data apart from Abstention-RL 5K in this paper traces back to one of three problem pools. Table 9 summarizes sizes, sources, and downstream consumers; the per-pool details follow.

Pool 1: DAPO-Math 5K.

We start from the public DAPO-Math [88] training split (14,11614{,}116 problems). Each problem is difficulty-stratified using the convention above, then we run the teacher in single-shot mode (T=0.3T{=}0.3, one rollout per problem) to produce one chain-of-thought trace ending in a boxed final answer. Traces whose final answer fails the two-stage verification are discarded. The remaining correct traces are quota-sampled per difficulty bucket (Table 10, left block) to a total of 4,7424{,}742 unique (problem, teacher-trace) instances. Separately, we sample 325325 additional verified traces as a validation set for monitoring the supervised loss.

Pool 2: DAPO++SimpleRL 8K.

This pool corresponds to the problem set introduced in Section 3.1.1: 8,5568{,}556 math problems drawn from the DAPO Math and SimpleRL-Zoo training set [89], curated via UR2 [47], stratified into the four difficulty buckets defined above, and rebalanced by down-sampling the two extreme buckets (easy and very_hard buckets) to 2,0002{,}000 each (Table 10, middle block). On top of these 8,5568{,}556 problems, we additionally build an expanded answer pool that is shared between several downstream datasets: we run the teacher in multi-shot mode (T=0.7T{=}0.7, 1212 rollouts per problem, ∼102,672\sim\!102{,}672 total), keep the rollouts whose final answer passes verification (∼89,104\sim\!89{,}104 correct traces, overall correctness ∼87%\sim\!87\%). This expanded answer pool is the upstream of (i) the SFT-80K corpus, which subsamples 70,35270{,}352 correct traces from it (§B.4.3), and (ii) the DPO-235B preference pool, which forms correct-vs-incorrect and short-vs-long pairs from the same 1212-rollout set (§F.1.3).

Pool 3: OpenMath (cleaned and difficulty-balanced 8K).

We additionally construct a cleaned non-MCQ subset from NVIDIA’s OpenMathReasoning [56]. Starting from 38,27238{,}272 non-MCQ problems, the cleaning pipeline retains 33,80133{,}801 problems (88.3%88.3\% retention). Appendix G.2 reports the full cleaning protocol, including which problems are removed, why they are removed, and the per-category removal breakdown. From the 33,80133{,}801 cleaned problems we then difficulty-balance the pool by random-sampling 2,0002{,}000 problems from each of the four difficulty buckets (seed 4242), yielding the final 8,0008{,}000-problem pool that is actually used downstream. Pool 3 is used only by the CPT 2×2\times scaling variant and DPO-small; none of the other datasets in this paper draws from it.

B.4.2 Math-SFT (∼10\sim\!10K)

The Math-SFT corpus used as the SFT/SFT+RL baseline in the main results is the simplest of all our datasets: it is exactly Pool 1, with each (problem, teacher-trace) instance duplicated twice. The on-disk training file therefore contains 9,4849{,}484 rows backed by 4,7424{,}742 unique items.

B.4.3 SFT-80K

The volume-matched SFT-80K corpus is built by concatenating the Math-SFT file with a 70,35270{,}352-row uniform random subsample of Pool 2’s expanded answer pool (∼89,104\sim\!89{,}104 verified-correct teacher traces). The total is 79,83679{,}836 items. Two design points are worth noting. The corpus is entirely answerable-math: it contains no abstention items, false-premise items, or non-math content.

B.4.4 CPT Data Construction Details

Section 3.1 gives the high-level three-stage CPT construction pipeline. Table 11 summarizes the full construction statistics; below we document implementation details omitted from the main text but required to reproduce the dataset exactly.

Problem-pool curation and difficulty balancing.

CPT uses the Pool 2 seed problem set (§B.4.1), namely the DAPO++SimpleRL 8K pool described above.

Rollout verification.

For each sampled rollout, we extract the final answer and determine correctness with a two-stage verifier: math_verify first, followed by a GPT-4.1-mini semantic-equivalence fallback when rule matching fails. These correctness labels are used only for constructing and stratifying pairs; the CPT model itself is trained from teacher-judge comparisons rather than from these verifier outputs directly.

Self-consistency filtering and judge-mode conversion.

For each pair z=(x,a∗,τA,τB)z=(x,a^{\ast},\tau^{A},\tau^{B}), the teacher judge produces K=8K{=}8 independent judgments, and we keep the pair only when at least τ=5\tau{=}5 judgments agree on the same label. We then sample 10,000 pairs from the consensus-retained pool and keep the highest-confidence teacher outputs for judge-mode SFT, filtering empty, invalid, or overlong examples.

Weighted sampling for intra-model pairs.

When two rollouts of the same model are paired (the intra-model strategy of §3.1.2), we use weighted sampling rather than uniform sampling. Correct rollouts receive weight 33 and incorrect rollouts receive weight 22, which increases the fraction of pairs that contain at least one correct trace and therefore the fraction of pairs that carry an informative teacher-judge signal.

Small-correct vs. large-incorrect: all ordered model-size combinations.

The third pair construction strategy (§3.1.2) is instantiated over all three ordered combinations of model sizes: 44B vs. 88B, 44B vs. 1414B, and 88B vs. 1414B. A pair is constructed only when the smaller model produces a verified-correct answer on a given problem and the larger model fails on the same problem; the three combinations together contribute the ∼12,886\sim\!12{,}886 “S​✓\text{S}\checkmark, L×\text{L}\times” pairs reported in Table 11.

Empirical four-way label distribution.

On a uniform 10,00010{,}000-pair sample of the consensus-retained pool, the teacher-judge’s verdict distribution is Path A better ∼43.7%\sim\!43.7\%, Path B better ∼46.2%\sim\!46.2\%, both equally bad ∼7.4%\sim\!7.4\%, both equally good ∼2.7%\sim\!2.7\%. The near-equal A::B ratio is a direct empirical check that the random position swap used during pair construction effectively removes positional bias in the upstream pair pool, leaving the teacher’s residual positional preference to be handled by self-consistency voting rather than by data balancing.

B.4.5 CPT Data Scaling

To probe whether the benefit of CPT continues to grow with more cognitive pairwise data, we evaluate two additional CPT data variants on Qwen3-14B-Base, alongside the main 1×1\times corpus described in §3.1. Both variants share the identical rollout, pair-construction, teacher-judge, and consensus-filter pipeline as 1×1\times; they differ only in the source pool and/or the sampling strategy. We use these two variants only in the data-scaling experiment of Table 30, never in the main results.

CPT 0.5×0.5\times Variant (35K)

The 0.5×0.5\times variant (35,17635{,}176 instances) is a uniform random subsample (seed 4242) of the main 1×1\times corpus: source pool, teacher-quality filtering, and seed-then-expand strategy are all unchanged. By construction it inherits the same ∼10\sim\!10K prompt-diversity ceiling as the 1×1\times corpus.

CPT 2×2\times Variant (140K)

The 2×2\times variant (140,704140{,}704 instances) differs from 1×1\times in exactly two coupled aspects — the underlying problem pool and the sampling strategy. Teacher-quality filters (consensus retention ++ max-confidence rollout) are identical to 1×1\times.

(a) Dual-source pool.

The 2×2\times corpus mixes pairs from two fully-judged pair pools, contributing 50%50\% each (Table 12):

  1. 1.

    DAPO++SimpleRL pair pool (Pool 2 above): the same pool used to build the main 1×1\times corpus (90,97090{,}970 pairs; 77,65777{,}657 consensus-retained).

  2. 2.

    OpenMath pair pool (Pool 3 above, 8,0008{,}000 cleaned and difficulty-balanced problems): pairs are constructed under the identical detailed pipeline (multi-model rollouts →\rightarrow debiased pair construction →\rightarrow teacher-judge labeling →\rightarrow confidence-based conversion), yielding 82,34382{,}343 pairs and 70,52070{,}520 consensus-retained pairs. Because OpenMath’s problem distribution is largely disjoint from DAPO++SimpleRL 8K, this half broadens topical and stylistic coverage.

(b) Expand-then-sample strategy.

The main 1×1\times corpus uses “seed-then-expand”: select ∼10\sim\!10K seed pairs, then expand each seed by its ∼7\sim\!7 tied-max-confidence rollouts, capping prompt diversity at ∼10\sim\!10K unique prompts. The 2×2\times corpus inverts this order:

  1. 1.

    Take all 148,177148{,}177 consensus-retained pairs across the two pools.

  2. 2.

    Expand each pair to its tied-max-confidence rollouts, yielding 996996K candidate (prompt, rollout) instances (511511K from the DAPO++SimpleRL half, 485485K from the OpenMath half).

  3. 3.

    Drop instances whose prompt+response\texttt{prompt}+\texttt{response} exceeds 12,28812{,}288 tokens under the Qwen3-14B-Base tokenizer (82+4982+49 instances dropped from the two halves respectively).

  4. 4.

    Sample 70,35270{,}352 instances uniformly at random from each half.

The methodological consequence is that every consensus-retained, max-confidence rollout becomes an independent sampling candidate, raising the prompt-diversity ceiling to ∼141\sim\!141K unique (prompt, rollout) combinations — a ∼⁣×\sim\!14\!\times jump over the main 1×1\times corpus at only 2×2\times the raw sample count.

Sanity checks of the 2×2\times corpus.

Label balance is preserved relative to 1×1\times (Path A 44.34%44.34\% / Path B 42.88%42.88\% / equally-bad 10.11%10.11\% / equally-good 2.67%2.67\% vs. 43.91/43.82/8.48/3.7943.91/43.82/8.48/3.79 at 1×1\times). Difficulty mix is hard​ 36.5%\texttt{hard}\,36.5\% / very_hard​ 26.3%\texttt{very\_hard}\,26.3\% / medium​ 20.9%\texttt{medium}\,20.9\% / easy​ 16.3%\texttt{easy}\,16.3\%. Pair-type mix is dominated by the design-time strategies of §3.1.2: intra-model 42.51%42.51\%, inter-model-different-correctness 33.10%33.10\%, inter-model-same-correctness 9.87%9.87\%, and the three small-correct/large-incorrect combinations 5.58+4.75+4.19=14.52%5.58+4.75+4.19=14.52\%. The per-instance prompt+response\texttt{prompt}+\texttt{response} character length has median 10,14310{,}143 and Q2525/Q7575 at 8,0958{,}095/12,56312{,}563.

B.4.6 SUM-SFT (Abstention SFT Baseline)

Source dataset and our role for it.

We build the unanswerable half of SUM-SFT on top of Synthetic Unanswerable Math (SUM) [72], which contains 36,48036{,}480 implicitly unanswerable math problems constructed from DeepScaleR [52] along five degradation axes (key-information deletion, ambiguous key information, unrealistic conditions, unrelated objects, question deletion). See the original paper for construction details. The raw SUM items ship with the hard label \boxed{I don’t know} but no chain-of-thought, so SFT’ing on them directly would teach the model the shortcut “always emit IDK”. We address this in two coupled steps. (i) Prompt rewriting for trace collection. The user prompt is rewritten to our standard two-class abstention template (Appendix D) so that the teacher’s reasoning naturally lands in \boxed{I don’t know} (information-insufficient) or \boxed{False premise} (false-premise). This rewriting is applied only when running the teacher; at training time the unanswerable half uses the same unified math prompt as the answerable half, with no abstention-permission hint, so that any abstention behavior comes purely from response-side supervision rather than from a prompt-side cue. (ii) Trace generation. For each rewritten prompt we run the teacher once under our standard single-shot setting (§B.4.1) and replace the hard label with the resulting trace.

Yield and answerable padding.

Of the 36,48036{,}480 rewritten prompts, 54.9%54.9\% of teacher rollouts end in IDK, 8.3%8.3\% in False-premise, 20.9%20.9\% in a confident specific answer, and 15.8%15.8\% are truncated without a valid boxed answer. We keep only the two abstention-token cases, yielding 23,05623{,}056 unanswerable training items with reasoning traces. To match the ∼80\sim\!80K volume of the other baselines, we add 56,78056{,}780 answerable math items from SFT-80K. The final SUM-SFT corpus has 79,83679{,}836 items. The downstream Math-RL stage is identical to our main pipeline. The resulting SUM-SFT++RL checkpoint has a much higher abstention rate than CPT+RL (e.g. 46.2%46.2\% vs. 26.1%26.1\% under the 14B Normal Prompt), which is consistent with its lower answerable-question accuracy in Figure 4.

B.4.7 DPO Pair Pools

The two DPO baselines used in the main results and Appendix F.1.3 are built directly on the seed pools above and we list only the source→\rightarrowpair mapping for completeness:

  • •

    DPO-235B (main). Source: the Pool-2 expanded answer pool (1212 teacher rollouts per problem at T=0.7T{=}0.7, ∼102\sim\!102K traces). Pairs: 37,14937{,}149 correct-vs-wrong (capped at 3030 per problem) ++ 33,70333{,}703 short-correct-vs-long-correct (for problems whose 1212 rollouts are all correct, top-33 shortest vs. top-33 longest, restricted to length ratio ≥1.5\geq\!1.5). Total 70,85270{,}852 pairs, 70,35270{,}352 train / 500/\,500 dev.

  • •

    DPO-small. Source: the same 44B/8/8B/14/14B Qwen3-Base rollout pool that feeds the CPT 1×1\times corpus (Pool 2 problems) plus its OpenMath analogue (Pool 3 problems). Pair construction follows §3.1.2 but uses a one-correct-one-incorrect filter on the verified-answer side rather than a teacher-judge label. Yields 36,878​(C​P​T)+ 30,944​(O​p​e​n​M​a​t​h)= 67,82236{,}878(CPT)\,+\,30{,}944(OpenMath)\,=\,67{,}822 pairs in total.

B.4.8 Abstention-RL 5K

We adopt the abstention-RL training set construction of Beyond I-Don’t-Know [65] without modification. Their pipeline starts from the DAPO-Math and uses a single LLM rewriter to derive, for each original answerable item, exactly one variant in one of two uncertainty regimes: information-insufficient variants, in which one or more critical conditions are deliberately removed or obscured, and extremely-difficult-but-well-defined variants, in which the problem is rewritten to be much harder to solve without external tools while remaining mathematically well-defined. Each rewritten variant is then verified by an independent LLM validator: insufficient variants must be judged “no unique solution” and extremely-difficult variants must be judged “has a unique solution”; up to five resamples per item are allowed before discarding. From this split, we select 2,5002{,}500 answerable problems, 1,2501{,}250 problems labeled “conflict”, and 1,2501{,}250 problems labeled “insufficient”.

We use this corpus verbatim, with one inherited convention: the answerable targets are scored as standard verifiable-math, while the two abstention-target classes are scored against the two abstention tokens used by the model’s response format — \boxed{I don’t know} for information-insufficient items and \boxed{False premise} for contradictory items. These two tokens align exactly with the two-class abstention prompt used by our base/instruct models at evaluation time (Appendix D); no further prompt engineering is applied. The answer reward is replaced with +1.0+1.0 for correctness on answerables and for issuing the correct abstention token on the two abstention classes; all other settings remain the same as in §B.1.

B.4.9 Math-RL Data

The Math-RL stage that every “++RL” baseline goes through is trained on a separate math-only problem set. It shares the same upstream source as Pool 2 (DAPO Math ++ SimpleRL-Zoo training set curated via UR2), but is assembled with a different balancing recipe and an explicit de-duplication against Pool 1: starting from the 22,17422{,}174-problem source, we down-sample the easy bucket to 2,0002{,}000, keep all medium / hard / very_hard problems (12,18612{,}186), and then remove the 3,5273{,}527 problems that overlap with Pool 1 (Math-SFT). This yields 10,65910{,}659 unique problems, heavily skewed toward harder difficulty levels (very_hard 66.7%66.7\%; rightmost block of Table 10). Following the original source of each problem, the pool is partitioned into two reward regimes for the RL stage: 7,9337{,}933 DAPO-Math problems are graded by the rule-based math_verify checker, while the remaining 2,7262{,}726 SimpleRL-Zoo problems additionally enable an LLM-as-judge fallback for cases where the rule-based check fails. No teacher rollouts are generated on this pool: it is consumed directly as a problem set during RL.

In summary, the non-RL corpora above draw from the three seed pools in Table 9, apply the shared difficulty stratification and teacher-temperature presets, and add either single-shot trace generation (Math-SFT, SUM-SFT), multi-shot expansion (SFT-80K), or pair construction with teacher-judge filtering (CPT, DPO). The two RL-only sets are consumed directly as prompts by their downstream policy-optimization stages.

Appendix C Evaluation Details

This section centralizes the evaluation data cards and scoring rules used in the paper. For all evaluations, models first reason and then place the final answer in \boxed{...}. Base checkpoints are prompted with a plain User:/Assistant: format; instruction-tuned checkpoints use their chat template. Unless a table explicitly reports multi-sample statistics, decoding is deterministic greedy decoding with temperature 00 and one rollout.

C.1 AbstentionBench

1. Dataset.

We use AbstentionBench [37] as the main metacognitive abstention benchmark. Each example contains a question, optional reference answers, a binary abstention label and metadata, the subset name, and an integer index:

{question, reference_answers, should_abstain, metadata, dataset, idx}.

A null or empty reference-answer field together with should_abstain=true marks a question on which the model should refuse, request clarification, or point out a false premise. After applying the official large-subset indices with a cap of 3,5003{,}500 items per subset, our merged evaluation file has 35,93535{,}935 examples across 2020 subsets. The subset type determines the correctness evaluator used after the abstention decision.

2. Rollout.

The main AbstentionBench runs use vLLM with temperature 00, maximum length 81928192, and one rollout. We evaluate two prompt regimes: Normal Prompt, which only requires a boxed final answer and contains no abstention hint, and Abstention Prompt, which additionally hints LLMs to use \boxed{I don’t know} and \boxed{False premise}. Normal-Prompt robustness variants are listed in Appendix F.2.1.

3. Evaluation pipeline.

Abstention detection is a two-stage hybrid procedure. First, a high-precision keyword path lowercases the final boxed answer and matches only abstention phrases that occur inside that box. The keyword inventory is: i don’t know, i do not know, false premise, incorrect assumption, unanswerable, unknown, unclear, uncertain, cannot be determined, can’t be determined, cannot be answered, can’t be answered, impossible to answer, impossible to determine, not enough information, insufficient information, no way to know, no way to determine, not possible to answer, not possible to determine, i cannot answer, i can’t answer, i cannot determine, i can’t determine, n/a, and not applicable. Items not caught by this fast path are judged by GPT-4.1-mini with a CoCoNot-style yes/no prompt that checks whether the full response is an abstention.

Correctness is evaluated only for examples with should_abstain=false and non-empty references. If an LLM abstains on such an answerable example, it is counted as incorrect. Otherwise, examples are routed by subset type: math subsets use boxed-answer extraction plus math_verify, with GPT-4.1-mini semantic equivalence as fallback; multiple-choice subsets extract an option letter and match it to the reference; free-form subsets use GPT-4.1-mini to judge the complete model response as correct or incorrect against the reference answers.

4. Metrics.

Let gi∈{0,1}g_{i}\in\{0,1\} denote the gold abstention label and pi∈{0,1}p_{i}\in\{0,1\} the predicted abstention decision. We compute

T​P=#⁡{gi=1,pi=1},F​P=#⁡{gi=0,pi=1},T​N=#⁡{gi=0,pi=0},F​N=#⁡{gi=1,pi=0}.TP=\#\{g_{i}=1,p_{i}=1\},\quad FP=\#\{g_{i}=0,p_{i}=1\},\quad TN=\#\{g_{i}=0,p_{i}=0\},\quad FN=\#\{g_{i}=1,p_{i}=0\}.

The abstention metrics are

Precision=T​PT​P+F​P,Recall=T​PT​P+F​N,F1=2​Precision​RecallPrecision+Recall,\mathrm{Precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\quad\mathrm{Recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN},\quad F_{1}=\frac{2\,\mathrm{Precision}\,\mathrm{Recall}}{\mathrm{Precision}+\mathrm{Recall}},

with abstention rate (T​P+F​P)/N(TP+FP)/N. For answerable examples, answerable-question accuracy (Acc-Ans) is

Accans=Cmath+Cchoice+CllmNmath+Nchoice+Nllm.\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{ans}}=\frac{C_{\mathrm{math}}+C_{\mathrm{choice}}+C_{\mathrm{llm}}}{N_{\mathrm{math}}+N_{\mathrm{choice}}+N_{\mathrm{llm}}}.

C.2 Mathematical Reasoning Tasks

1. Dataset.

We evaluate MATH-500 [30], OlympiadBench [28], Minerva Math [43], AMC 2022–2023 [2], and AIME 2024–2025 [1]. Each example provides at least a question and a gold answer; answers may be raw numbers, LaTeX expressions, units, or already boxed strings. The seven tasks are grouped in the main results into an Easy split and a Hard split as summarized below.

2. Rollout.

All seven tasks are run with a CoT-style math prompt that asks the model to solve step by step and put the final answer in \boxed{...}. We use vLLM with temperature 0.50.5, top-p=0.5p=0.5, top-k=10k=10, maximum length 81928192, and dataset-specific rollouts: N=2N=2 for MATH-500, Minerva Math, and OlympiadBench, and N=8N=8 for AMC 2022, AMC 2023, AIME 2024, and AIME 2025. The higher rollout count on AMC/AIME reduces variance on the small competition-test sets.

3. Evaluation pipeline.

For each generation, the evaluator extracts the last boxed answer; if no boxed answer exists, it records I don’t know., which is counted as wrong. The extracted prediction and the gold answer are wrapped in \boxed{} when needed and scored by math_verify with LaTeX/expression extraction. When math_verify returns 00, GPT-4.1-mini is used as a semantic-equivalence fallback only for MATH-500, Minerva Math and OlympiadBench; AMC and AIME are kept rule-only because their answers are simple integers or numeric strings.

4. Metrics.

For question qq with rollout scores sq,1,…,sq,N∈{0,1}s_{q,1},\ldots,s_{q,N}\in\{0,1\}, the primary reported statistic is the average accuracy over sampled rollouts,

accq=1N​∑r=1Nsq,r.\mathrm{acc}_{q}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{r=1}^{N}s_{q,r}.

Dataset scores are the mean of accq\mathrm{acc}_{q} over questions. The Easy, Hard, and Overall Math numbers in the paper are macro-averages over datasets: Easy averages the five Easy task scores, Hard averages the two Hard task scores, and Overall averages all seven task scores. Majority-vote and best-of-NN scores are logged only for analysis. Detailed tables are in Appendix F.1.2.

C.3 RAG-Conflict

1. Dataset.

We use the Conflicts [8] (RAG-Conflict benchmark) for cross-task generalization. It contains 458458 examples, each with a question, up to ten retrieved documents, a five-way conflict type, and a reference answer when one exists. The evaluation collapses the five original conflict types into three task types: answerable-normal combines No conflict (161161) and Conflict due to misinformation (55), since the false information in the latter cases is easy to identify and can be ignored, so we categorize them as this type; answerable-outdated is Conflict due to outdated information (6262), where the newest answer should be selected; and abstain combines Complementary information (115115) with Conflicting opinions and research outcomes (115115), where no single agreed answer exists.

2. Rollout.

All RAG examples use the same category-blind prompt (verbatim in Appendix D.1): the model first asks whether the references and its own knowledge support one agreed answer; if not, it must output \boxed{I don’t know}; if yes, it answers, using the most up-to-date source when references are outdated. In Table 4, we use N=8N=8 rollouts at temperature 1.01.0 to expose both average and best-of-NN behavior.

3. Evaluation pipeline.

The evaluator extracts the last \boxed{...} as pred_ans. Abstention is recognized only from this extracted answer, using a conservative regex over forms such as “I don’t know”, “unknown”, “no consensus”, “insufficient information”, “cannot answer”, “N/A”, and “abstain”. Empty extracted answers are not counted as abstentions. For abstain-type questions, a rollout is correct if the extracted answer is recognized as abstention. For answerable-normal and answerable-outdated questions, abstention is wrong; otherwise correctness is judged against correct_answer by token-F1 short-circuiting followed by GPT-4.1-mini LLM-as-a-judge for the remaining cases.

4. Metrics.

For question qq with rollout scores sq,1,…,sq,N∈{0,1}s_{q,1},\ldots,s_{q,N}\in\{0,1\}, we compute

avgq=1N∑r=1Nsq,r,bestq=𝟏[maxrsq,r=1].\mathrm{avg}_{q}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{r=1}^{N}s_{q,r},\quad\mathrm{best}_{q}=\mathbf{1}[\max_{r}s_{q,r}=1].

For any task type tt, the reported task accuracy is the mean of the corresponding per-question statistic over q∈Qtq\in Q_{t}; the overall score is the size-weighted mean over all 458458 questions.
